issues.legal_issue: A company acting as secretary and adviser to another company owes it fiduciary duties, but its purchase of that company’s assets is not impeachable for fiduciary gain when the transaction is shown to have been fair, fully informed, and free of concealed advantage.
material_facts: The purchaser was appointed secretary of the asset-owning company, handled its correspondence and accounts, assisted it and its shareholders in selling the estates, and acquired intimate knowledge of the properties.

The seller faced pressure to repay a secured bank debt and could not do so without selling assets; the shareholders knowingly chose an offer that allowed them to retain an estate they wanted to keep while liquidating the debt.
The shareholders were competent, knew the properties and their value, unanimously accepted the proposal, obtained legal advice, and agreed to documents found to be in proper legal form.

The court found the price fair, no material information had been concealed or used to secure an advantage, and there was no fraud, undue influence, or conflict that produced pecuniary gain for the purchaser.
The shareholders made no complaint about the sale for twelve years.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser stood in a fiduciary relationship to the seller and should have avoided entering the transaction, but it proved that the sale was just and fair and that it gained no pecuniary advantage by using its fiduciary position; the transaction was not impeachable on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: A person in a fiduciary character must not place personal interest in conflict with duty and must hold for the beneficiary any pecuniary advantage gained through that character (Trusts Act, 1882, s. 88). A fiduciary is not absolutely incapable of buying from the beneficiary, but bears the burden of affirmatively proving a distinct and fair transaction, full understanding and information on the beneficiary’s part, a just price, and absence of fraud, concealment, or use of fiduciary information. Coles v. Trecothick, 9 Ves. Jun. 234, 247; Parks v. White, 11 Ves. Jun. 209, 226.

rule.if: fiduciary_asset_purchase_dispute and secretary_managed_seller_affairs and seller_fully_informed and seller_knew_asset_value and fair_price_accepted and no_concealment_or_undue_influence and no_fiduciary_information_used

predicates.fiduciary_asset_purchase_dispute: The dispute concerns a company secretary purchasing assets from the company whose affairs it served.
predicates.secretary_managed_seller_affairs: The purchaser handled the seller’s correspondence and accounts and assisted the seller in arranging a sale.
predicates.seller_fully_informed: The seller understood that it was dealing with the purchaser and had the material information about the transaction.
predicates.seller_knew_asset_value: The seller knew the value of the assets and considered the available offers.
predicates.fair_price_accepted: The seller accepted a price the court found just and fair in the circumstances.
predicates.no_concealment_or_undue_influence: The transaction involved no concealment, fraud, or undue influence.
predicates.no_fiduciary_information_used: The purchaser did not use information obtained through its fiduciary role to gain an advantage.

issues.definition: When a company secretary purchases assets from a company whose affairs it served, a fully informed sale at a fair price without concealment, undue influence, or use of fiduciary information results in a fair transaction without fiduciary gain.

issues.legal_issue: A beneficiary’s claim for relief concerning trust property is subject to the applicable limitation period when the property was not held specifically for transfer to the beneficiary and fraud has not been established.
material_facts: The claim sought declarations, transfer or reconveyance of property, and accounts concerning assets conveyed to a new company.
The claimants did not establish the alleged fraud, so the court found the fraud-based limitation provision inapplicable.
The properties were not vested in the new company for the specific purpose of making them over to the old company or the claimants.
The cause of action arose when the conveyances to the new company were made, and the suit was brought more than six years later.
The plaint did not seek recovery of possession; the court also held that even if the claim were treated as one for possession, the same limitation rule applied.
issues.conclusion: The suit was barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: Article 120 of the Limitation Act, 1908 governed the claim, with six years running from the cause of action. Article 95 did not apply because fraud was not established; s. 10 did not apply because the property was not held for the specific purpose of making it over to the beneficiaries; and Article 144 did not govern the claim. A beneficiary cannot avoid the limitation period for enforcing the right to call on a trustee to convey by later bringing a possessory claim. Rani Chhatra Kumari Devi v. Prince Mohan Bikram Shah, L.R. 58 I.A. 279.

rule.if: beneficiary_trust_property_claim and property_not_held_specifically_for_beneficiary and no_proven_fraud and cause_of_action_accrued_on_transfer and claim_brought_more_than_six_years_after_accrual

predicates.beneficiary_trust_property_claim: The claimant seeks relief concerning property held or claimed for a beneficiary.
predicates.property_not_held_specifically_for_benef: The property was not placed with its holder for the specific purpose of transferring it to the claimant or beneficiary.
predicates.no_proven_fraud: The claimant did not establish fraud supporting the claim.
predicates.cause_of_action_accrued_on_transfer: The claim arose when the property was conveyed to its current holder.
predicates.claim_brought_more_than_six_years_after_: The claimant brought suit more than six years after the cause of action accrued.

issues.definition: A beneficiary’s trust-property claim is barred when it was brought more than six years after the cause accrued on transfer, the property was not held specifically for transfer to the beneficiary, and fraud was not established.

issues.legal_issue: Shareholders or creditors cannot maintain an action to recover a dissolved company’s assets when the dissolution remains effective and no applicable law transfers those assets to them.
material_facts: The company completed voluntary winding up and stood dissolved under the Indian Companies Act, 1913.
No application was made within the statutory period to have the dissolution declared void, and the claimants failed to establish fraud affecting the dissolution.
The claimants were shareholders seeking recovery of assets belonging to the dissolved company; the company itself was not able to receive the assets through the action.
The governing law contained no provision vesting the dissolved company’s property in a trustee for its shareholders or creditors, or otherwise transferring it to them.
issues.conclusion: The shareholders were not entitled to maintain the suit; the dissolved company’s property, if any, vested in the Government by escheat or as bona vacantia, and the assets could not be restored to the company through the action.
issues.legal_principle: The right of the Government to take property by escheat or as bona vacantia is an incident of sovereignty. Article 296 of the Constitution and the earlier Government of India enactments recognize that right; under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, winding up precedes dissolution, and the Act supplied no mechanism vesting the dissolved company’s assets in a trustee for shareholders or creditors. Sections 209H and 243 of that Act governed dissolution and the possibility of setting it aside. Collector of Masulipatam v. C. Vencata Narainapah, 8 M.I.A. 500, 525; Bombay Dyeing and Manufacturing Co. v. State of Bombay, [1958] S.C.R. 1122, 1146; Legal Remembrancer v. Corporation of Calcutta, [1967] 2 S.C.R. 170, 204; In re U.N. Mandal’s Estate, A.I.R. 1959 Cal. 493, 498; In re Wells, [1933] 1 Ch. 29; Coxon v. Gorst, [1891] 2 Ch. 73; In re Lewis and Smart Ltd., [1954] 1 W.L.R. 755.

predicates.shareholder_or_creditor_asset_recovery_a: Shareholders or creditors brought an action to recover assets that belonged to a company.
predicates.company_dissolved: The company completed winding up and its dissolution took effect.
predicates.no_fraud_invalidating_dissolution: The claimants did not establish fraud that invalidated the dissolution.
predicates.no_law_transfers_residual_assets_to_memb: No applicable law transferred the dissolved company’s residual assets to its shareholders or creditors or vested them in a representative for those claimants.

issues.definition: When shareholders or creditors seek a dissolved company’s assets, an effective dissolution, no established fraud invalidating it, and no law transferring the assets to the claimants mean they cannot maintain the recovery action.
